questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The force a flying buttress takes
questions.learningObjective: Identify the force a flying buttress carries to the outer pier
questions.stem: A field station log lists the buttress piers of a surveyed church and notes a heavy masonry mass standing clear of the wall, with a raking arch running from the vault springing down to it. What is that element doing?

options.text: It carries the vault's outward thrust out to the outer pier, where the mass of the pier balances it
It props the aisle wall against the inward push of the vault, so the wall can stay thinner
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the vault's thrust

options.text: It collects rainwater from the vault springing and channels it down into the drain at the pier
options.misconception: treats the buttress as a drainage device

options.text: It steadies the vault during the years when the centring was struck and the ribs stood alone
options.misconception: gives the buttress a temporary centring role

questions.explanation: The flying buttress takes the vault's horizontal thrust at the springing and carries it to an outer pier, whose weight resists the overturning. It does not push the wall back inward.
questions.hint: Ask which way the vault pushes.

questions.topic: Why a tensioned concrete beam spans further
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the compressive stress imposed by prestressing tendons
questions.stem: The camp survey records prestressing tendons in a beam section of 0.25 square metres being tensioned to a force of 600 kN. What compressive stress in kilopascals is this force applied to the concrete section?
questions.explanation: The compressive stress is tendon force over section area: 600 kN over 0.25 square metres gives 2400 kPa. The tendons are the only source of this compression, so their force sets the stress.
questions.hint: Divide the tendon force by the area.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a column has base, shaft and capital
questions.learningObjective: Identify which part of a column spreads the load from the beam

stimulus.body: A survey record describes a column at a coastal site. The lowest element is a square plinth a little wider than the shaft, carrying a shallow rounded moulding. Above that the shaft rises for the full height of the bay, plain and slightly tapered. At the top it meets a flaring block that spreads out to meet a horizontal beam resting on it. The note asks the survey team which of the three parts spreads the load from the beam above.

questions.stem: Which part of the surveyed column spreads the load from the beam above down into the shaft?

options.text: The plinth at the foot, which spreads the beam's load through the length of the shaft
options.misconception: credits the base with spreading the load from above

options.text: The capital, the flaring block at the top, which passes the beam's load evenly into the shaft
The shaft itself, which tapers so that the load from the beam is carried along its length
options.misconception: credits the taper rather than the capital

options.text: The rounded moulding, which cushions the shock of the beam settling on the column
options.misconception: treats the moulding as an impact cushion

questions.explanation: The capital is the transition between the wide beam and the narrow shaft, so it spreads the load across the shaft. The base spreads the load into the ground, and the shaft carries the compression.
questions.hint: Think of the element between beam and shaft.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What distinguishes the three classical orders
questions.learningObjective: Identify the order from the absence of a base and a plain capital
questions.stem: A sketch made in the survey tent shows a column with no base and a simple cushion capital. Which order does that combination indicate?

options.text: Corinthian, whose carved leaves are reduced to a plain cushion when the column is short
options.misconception: imagines Corinthian capitals reduced to cushions

options.text: Ionic, whose scrolls are simplified on small buildings and whose base can be left out
options.misconception: treats a simplified Ionic as having no base

options.text: Doric, whose plain capital and base-less shaft set it apart from the two more slender orders
Tuscan, which is a later plain variant and is always found without a base
options.misconception: confuses the plain Roman variant with Doric

questions.explanation: A base-less shaft with a simple cushion capital is the giveaway of the Doric order, whose shaft is stouter at about six diameters. Ionic and Corinthian stand on moulded bases with decorated capitals.
questions.hint: Ask which order has no base.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A colonnade on three sides
questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of a covered walk running round a building
questions.stem: In a short field brief, explain how a colonnade on three sides changes the experience of walking around a building.

answer.exemplar: A colonnade on three sides creates a covered walk that runs along the front and returns down both flanks, so the whole building is experienced at close range rather than as a single front seen from a distance. The columns stand between the walker and the wall, filtering the daylight and the sound of the street, so the building feels separated from the outside without becoming sealed off from it. At the far ends of the returns the walk stops and the solid wall of the cella takes over, which is what makes the passage feel like a deliberate sequence rather than an endless corridor.

questions.explanation: A colonnade on three sides makes a covered walk along the front and both flanks, so the building is experienced close up with filtered light and sound. The walk ends at the solid cella wall, making a sequence.
questions.hint: Think about walking round the building.

questions.stem: A table of measured column bases from the survey gives three podiums with heights of 1.1 m, 2.4 m and 4.0 m above the surrounding ground. What does the variation suggest about the site?

options.text: The variation reflects the depth of the foundations rather than the level of the ground
options.misconception: reads podium height as foundation depth

options.text: The buildings were raised by later generations to protect them from rising damp over time
options.misconception: explains podium height by later damp protection

options.text: The tallest podium belongs to the largest building, since the platform scales with the size of the temple
options.misconception: ties podium height to building size

options.text: The ground falls away steeply, so each building needs a different lift to bring its platform level

questions.explanation: A constant podium height would suggest level ground, while podiums that rise as the ground falls show each platform was levelled individually. These differences point to a sloping site, not to size.
questions.hint: Compare the podiums with the ground.

questions.topic: What the pediment closes
questions.learningObjective: Identify what the pediment closes and what its field carries
questions.stem: Two questions are put to the survey team: what the triangle above the entrance actually closes, and what its flat inner field is used for.

options.text: It closes the top of the cella wall, and the flat field inside the frame admits the only light
options.misconception: treats the pediment as a light source

options.text: It closes the open end of the timber roof, and the flat field inside the frame carries the relief
It closes the gap between the two roof slopes, and the flat field inside the frame is left unpainted
options.misconception: misidentifies the gable as a roof junction

options.text: It closes the water tank behind the roof, and the flat field inside the frame is used as a shelf
options.misconception: invents a tank behind the roof

questions.explanation: The gable end of a timber roof is an open triangle of rafters, and the pediment closes it with a finished masonry face. Its flat inner field, the tympanum, receives the sculpture of the front.
questions.hint: Look at what the rafters hide.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The force a flying buttress takes
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the pier weight needed to balance a buttress overturning moment
questions.stem: The survey team measures a flying buttress whose outer pier has a resisting lever arm of 1.5 m from the toe, while the vault thrust of 45 kN arrives at 6 m above the base. What weight in kN must the pier have to balance the moment?
questions.explanation: The overturning moment is thrust times height, 45 x 6 = 270 kN metres. The pier must match it with weight times lever arm, so W = 270 / 1.5 = 180 kN.
questions.hint: Balance thrust times height against weight times arm.

questions.topic: Why a tensioned concrete beam spans further
questions.learningObjective: Describe the structural job of a prestressing tendon
questions.stem: When the survey team measures a prestressed concrete footbridge, they find a tendon running the full length of the beam and anchored at both ends. Which statement best describes its job?

options.text: It replaces the reinforcement that would otherwise resist the tension caused by the traffic load
options.misconception: claims the tendon removes the need for ordinary steel

options.text: It suspends the beam from the anchors, so the middle of the span hangs instead of bending
options.misconception: treats the tendon as a hanger rather than a tie

options.text: It pulls the beam into compression so that the load it carries does not create tension at the soffit
It shortens the effective span of the beam by connecting the two supports at deck level
options.misconception: treats the tendon as a deck level tie

questions.explanation: The tendon is stretched and anchored, so it pulls the beam ends inward and compresses the concrete. That compression offsets the tension that would open the soffit, so the beam can be shallower.
questions.hint: Ask what the tendon does to the concrete.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a column has base, shaft and capital
questions.learningObjective: Recognise a slender load-bearing column from its taper and fluting

stimulus.body: A survey of a ruined hall records two column shafts. The first is very slightly tapered, wider at the foot than at the top, and its fluting is cut into a surface that is plainly not perfectly true. The second shaft is shorter in proportion and its stone shows tool marks running straight up its face. The note asks the survey team which shaft is more likely to have been the slender load-bearing one in its original state.

questions.stem: Which of the two recorded shafts is more consistent with a slender, load-bearing column?

options.text: Neither, because the difference between the two shafts is only the quality of the tool marks
options.misconception: ignores the taper as evidence

options.text: The second, since the straight tool marks show it was dressed with care by a skilled workshop
options.misconception: reads workmanship quality as structural evidence

options.text: The second, since a shorter shaft is automatically better at resisting the load it carries
options.misconception: believes shortness always improves load resistance

options.text: The first, since its slight taper and the way its fluting follows the shaft suit a structural column

questions.explanation: A slender column tapers so the section is largest at the foot, where the bending moment is greatest, and the fluting follows the curve of the shaft. Tool marks alone say nothing about its role.
questions.hint: Look at the shape of the shaft, not the finish.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What distinguishes the three classical orders
questions.learningObjective: Recognise the Doric ratio from measured heights and diameters
questions.stem: A table of column heights gives, for three columns, shaft diameters of 0.60, 0.55 and 0.50 m and total heights of 3.6, 4.4 and 5.0 m. Which set of measurements indicates the Doric order?

options.text: The second column, whose height is eight times its diameter, the ratio that marks the Doric order
options.misconception: confuses the Ionic ratio with the Doric one

options.text: The first column, whose height is six times its diameter, the ratio that marks the Doric order
The third column, whose height is ten times its diameter, the ratio that marks the Doric order
options.misconception: confuses the Corinthian ratio with the Doric one

options.text: All three columns, because the three ratios together cover the three classical orders equally
options.misconception: treats three different ratios as one identical order

questions.explanation: The ratios are 3.6 over 0.60, which is 6, and 4.4 over 0.55, which is 8, and 5.0 over 0.50, which is 10. Six diameters is the Doric proportion, eight is Ionic and ten is Corinthian.
questions.hint: Divide each height by its diameter.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A colonnade on three sides
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a colonnade returns along both flanks
questions.stem: In a field note on the portico, explain why a colonnade was built along the front and down both sides rather than only across the front.

answer.exemplar: A row of columns across the front alone would read as a screen standing in front of the building, and the returns along the flanks would remain blank walls. Running the colonnade down both sides turns the front into a covered walk that can be followed all the way round the building, so the enclosure is experienced continuously rather than as a single elevation. It also shelters the side walls from the sun, which matters greatly in a hot climate, and it carries the roof edge over a wall that would otherwise have to be thickened. The three-sided arrangement is therefore both an architectural gesture and a practical response to climate.

questions.explanation: A colonnade down both flanks turns the front into a walk round the building, shelters the side walls from the sun and carries the roof edge over them. A single front row would leave the returns blank.
questions.hint: Think about walking round the building.

questions.topic: What a podium and a single stair achieve
questions.learningObjective: State what a podium and a single stair each contribute

options.text: The platform protects the columns from the rain, and the stair hides the entrance behind a screen of steps
options.misconception: treats the stair as a screen rather than an approach

options.text: The platform raises the building so it can be seen from farther away, and the stair lets people enter from the side
options.misconception: credits the stair with side entry

options.text: The platform gives the building a clear base above the ground, and the stair makes one formal approach to it
The platform stores water beneath the building, and the stair drains it away through a channel
options.misconception: treats the podium as a water store

questions.explanation: A podium lifts the building clear of the ground, giving a settled base line, protecting the lowest courses from damp and dramatising the approach. A broad stair concentrates the approach on one axis and one doorway.
questions.hint: Think about base and approach.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the area of the triangular field inside a pediment
questions.stem: The survey team's second measurement covers the tympanum of a pediment whose base is 6 m wide and whose apex stands 1.2 m above the horizontal cornice. What is the area of that triangular field in square metres?
questions.explanation: The tympanum is a triangle of base 6 m and height 1.2 m, so its area is half the product, 0.5 x 6 x 1.2 = 3.6 square metres. Treating the pediment as a rectangle would wrongly give 7.2.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why a flying buttress is a raking arch and not a solid mass
questions.stem: A camp survey notes that the flying buttress is built as a thin raking arch rather than as a solid triangular mass of masonry. Which statement best explains the choice?

options.text: The thin arch allows daylight to reach the aisle wall, which a solid mass would have blocked
options.misconception: gives daylight as the reason for the arch form

options.text: A solid mass would be far more expensive to build in the local stone, so the thin arch was a saving
options.misconception: gives economy as the reason for the arch form

options.text: A thin raking arch can span the gap to the pier without any intermediate support beneath it
options.misconception: treats the thin arch as a convenience for spanning

options.text: The raking curve keeps the thrust running down the buttress in compression, so a thin section is enough

questions.explanation: The buttress works as an arch cut in half, so its curve keeps the thrust in compression and a slim section carries it. A solid mass of the same height would resist by weight alone, at far greater cost.

questions.topic: Why a tensioned concrete beam spans further
questions.learningObjective: Explain why prestressing allows a shallower beam
questions.stem: Under a survey plan for a long hall, the team proposes a prestressed concrete roof instead of a plain reinforced one. What advantage does the survey note record?

options.text: The tendons allow the concrete to be mixed with less cement, which lowers the cost of the pour
options.misconception: credits the mix rather than the stress state

options.text: The tendons keep the concrete compressed, so the beam can be shallower and reach further between supports
The tendons absorb the expansion of the concrete as the temperature of the hall changes
options.misconception: treats the tendons as movement joints

options.text: The tendons allow the beam to be cast without any reinforcement mesh, since they replace it entirely
options.misconception: believes tendons eliminate ordinary reinforcement

questions.explanation: Prestressing holds the concrete in compression so flexural tension at the soffit never develops. The section no longer has to be sized for that tension, so it can be shallower for the same span.
questions.hint: Think about what the tendons do to the tension.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the bearing pressure imposed by a column base
questions.stem: The survey records a column base of 1.0 square metre carrying a concentrated load of 450 kN from the shaft above. What bearing pressure in kilopascals does the base impose on the floor?
questions.explanation: Bearing pressure is the load over the bearing area: 450 kN divided by 1.0 square metre gives 450 kPa. A base of half that area would double the pressure, and a base of twice the area would halve it.
questions.hint: Divide the load by the bearing area.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What distinguishes the three classical orders
questions.learningObjective: Identify an order from a written description of its capital

stimulus.body: A survey card records three column types at a temple ruin. The first has no base, a fluted shaft with sharp ridges between the flutes and a simple rounded capital, and measures six times its own diameter in height. The second has a base, a slender shaft and a capital carved with scrolls, at eight diameters. The third has a base, a slender shaft and a capital surrounded by carved leaves, at ten diameters.

questions.stem: Which column on the survey card is Corinthian, and what tells it apart?

options.text: The second, because a capital carved with scrolls and a base mark the Corinthian order
options.misconception: names the Ionic column as the Corinthian one

options.text: The first, because the absence of a base and the plain capital mark the oldest of the orders
options.misconception: names the Doric column as the Corinthian one

options.text: The third, because a capital carved with leaves and a ratio of ten diameters mark the Corinthian order
None of them, because the Corinthian order is defined by its fluting and not by its capital
options.misconception: believes Corinthian is defined by its fluting

questions.explanation: Corinthian is identified by a capital of carved leaves and a slender shaft of about ten diameters. Doric has no base and a plain capital at six diameters, while Ionic has scrolls at eight.
questions.hint: Look for leaves or scrolls on the capital.

options.text: The columns hold up a second storey that has since been lost, so the walk is really a balcony

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a podium and a single stair achieve
questions.learningObjective: Explain the purpose of a podium beneath a classical building
questions.stem: In a field note on the temple platform, explain why the whole building was raised on a podium rather than set directly on the ground.

answer.exemplar: A podium lifts the whole building clear of the ground on a level artificial platform, so the columns stand on a known, even surface instead of following the slope of the site. It also keeps ground damp and rising water away from the lowest courses of masonry, which is why so many ancient buildings show decay first at the foot. Architecturally it gives the building a firm horizontal base against which the columns can be read as a row, and it lets the whole front be seen from one standing position.

questions.explanation: A podium sets the building on a level platform, keeps damp away from the lowest courses and gives the columns a firm horizontal base. Setting the building on uneven ground would tilt the row of columns.
questions.hint: Think about level, damp and base line.

questions.topic: What distinguishes the three classical orders
questions.learningObjective: Identify the frieze band within a classical entablature

stimulus.body: A survey of a temple front records a horizontal cornice above the columns carried on plain blocks, and above it a second band ornamented with alternating figures and round shields. Above the second band a row of small tooth-like blocks runs along the front, and the whole is capped by a shallow triangular pediment. The note asks the survey team to record which band of the entablature carries the alternating figures and shields.

questions.stem: Which band of the entablature carries the alternating figures and round shields in the survey?

options.text: The architrave, the plain lowest band that sits directly on top of the column capitals
options.misconception: names the plain lowest band as the figured one

options.text: The frieze, the middle band of the entablature, above the architrave and below the cornice
The cornice, the crowning band whose projecting blocks form the shadow line at the top
options.misconception: names the crowning band as the figured one

options.text: The tympanum, the triangular field enclosed by the sloping cornices of the pediment
options.misconception: places the figures in the pediment field

questions.explanation: The entablature has three bands: architrave at the bottom, frieze in the middle, cornice on top. Figures and shields belong to the frieze, and the tooth-like blocks are the dentils of the cornice.
questions.hint: Name the three bands of the entablature.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A colonnade on three sides
questions.learningObjective: Interpret daylight readings taken inside a covered walk
questions.stem: A table of colonnade readings from the site gives, for three walks, a depth of 2.4 m with a measured daylight factor of 6 per cent, a depth of 1.2 m with 3 per cent, and a depth of 3.6 m with 9 per cent. What does the table show?

options.text: The readings are unrelated to depth, since a colonnade blocks light whatever its proportions
options.misconception: claims light is unaffected by the walk depth

options.text: Light inside the walk falls with its depth, so a deeper colonnade admits less light to the wall
options.misconception: reverses the trend shown by the readings

options.text: Light inside the walk rises with its depth, so a deeper colonnade shades the wall more completely
The readings show that width, not depth, sets how much light reaches the covered walk
options.misconception: attributes the readings to width rather than depth

questions.explanation: The readings pair a doubling of depth with a doubling of the daylight factor, so a deeper walk passes more sky light down to the wall behind. Depth, not width, is what the survey picks out.
questions.hint: Look for the pattern as depth doubles.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a podium and a single stair achieve
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a single axial stair is preferred to several approaches
questions.stem: In a discussion of the surveyed platform, explain why a single broad stair was used rather than several smaller ones at different points.

answer.exemplar: Several small stairs would let people arrive from anywhere, which breaks the clear relationship between the front of the building and the way it is approached. A single broad stair on the central axis fixes one line of sight and one line of movement, so the columns, the doorway and the viewer are all arranged on the same line. The stair also has to match the width of the portico, which is why it is broad rather than a narrow side entrance, and it turns the act of arrival into the first part of the building's design.

questions.explanation: A single broad stair on the central axis fixes one line of sight and movement, so columns, doorway and viewer line up. Several small stairs would break that arrangement and let the front be approached from anywhere.
questions.hint: Think about the axis of the front.

options.text: To hold a row of statues along the roof edge of the temple

options.text: To carry the weight of the roof rafters down into the walls at the two ends of the building
options.misconception: credits the cornice with a structural load path

options.text: To drain rainwater off the gable into a channel above the front door
options.misconception: treats the cornice as a rainwater channel

options.text: To throw a strong shadow that frames the tympanum and makes the whole gable read as one shape

questions.explanation: A projecting cornice throws a deep shadow, and that shadow makes the pediment read as a single framed shape against the sky. The cornice carries nothing structural and is not a drainage channel.

questions.stem: The survey team resolves a discrepancy in two notes of the same springing. One records a vertical component of 30 kN and the other a horizontal component of 40 kN. What is the magnitude of the resultant thrust in kN?
questions.explanation: The resultant is the square root of the sum of the squares of the components: the square root of 30 squared plus 40 squared is 50 kN. Adding the components instead would wrongly give 70 kN.
questions.hint: Use the square root of the sum of squares.

questions.topic: Why a tensioned concrete beam spans further
questions.learningObjective: Explain why prestressing tendons must be anchored
questions.stem: A junior surveyor asks why prestressing tendons must be anchored firmly at the ends of a beam rather than simply stopped. Which answer is correct?

options.text: Because the anchor prevents the concrete from cracking as it cools and shrinks during curing
options.misconception: credits the anchor with controlling shrinkage cracking

options.text: Because the prestress only exists while the tendon is stretched between two anchors that hold it
Because the anchorage spreads the prestress over a wider length of the beam than a bond alone
options.misconception: describes anchorage as a bond length device

options.text: Because an unanchored tendon would be pulled back into the duct and lost inside the beam
options.misconception: invents a duct beyond the beam ends

questions.explanation: Prestress is the tension held in the tendon by its anchors. Without anchorage the tendon would shorten and the compression in the concrete would vanish, so the technique depends on holding the ends.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why capitals and bases are wider than the shaft

options.text: It reduces the weight of the column by hollowing the ends, which lightens the structure below
options.misconception: invents a hollowing effect in the ends

options.text: It makes the column look uniform from bottom to top, hiding the change of load at each end
options.misconception: gives the flare a purely visual purpose

options.text: It spreads the load from the entablature and into the ground, while keeping the shaft itself slender
It channels rainwater from the capital down through a hollow in the shaft to the base
options.misconception: invents a drainage channel in the shaft

questions.explanation: The capital is where the wide entablature hands its load to the narrow shaft, and the base is where the shaft hands it to the floor. Flaring both ends spreads the load at the transitions.

options.text: An open courtyard with no roof at all, the stone bench being the only remaining structure
options.misconception: ignores the continuous roof recorded in the note

options.text: A storeroom enclosed by the columns, with the wall behind serving as its outer face
options.misconception: treats the walk as an enclosed room

options.text: A covered walk between the columns and the wall, sheltered from the sun and open to the street

questions.explanation: The continuous roof over the space between the columns and the wall shows it is a covered walk, and the bench confirms it is meant to be occupied. It is open to the street and closed by the wall behind.

Three courses of stone were simply the unit the local masons could quarry and lift

options.misconception: invents a lighting rule for the platform height

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the pediment closes
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a classical front needs a pediment
questions.stem: In a design review at the field station, explain why a classical building needs a pediment on its front rather than leaving the roof end plain.

answer.exemplar: The end of a timber roof is an open triangle of rafters and purlins, which cannot be left exposed without showing the structure and letting rain and wind into the building. A pediment closes that end with a triangle of masonry whose horizontal cornice carries the lines of the orders forward and whose sloping sides echo the pitch of the roof. Its flat inner field, the tympanum, is the natural place for a relief, and the height of the gable also sets the proportion of the roof to the whole front.

questions.explanation: The open triangle of the timber roof end must be closed, and the pediment closes it with a finished triangular face whose cornices continue the lines of the orders. Its tympanum gives a field for sculpture.
questions.hint: Think about the exposed roof end.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The force a flying buttress takes
questions.learningObjective: Compare the overturning margin of three buttress piers
questions.stem: A measurement table from the site gives three outer piers. Pier one resists a 30 kN thrust 5 m up with a weight of 200 kN and a 1.2 m lever arm; pier two resists 45 kN at 6 m with 240 kN and 1.5 m; pier three resists 20 kN at 4 m with 150 kN and 1.3 m. Which is least secure?

options.text: Pier three, because its light pier has the smallest weight to resist any overturning at all
options.misconception: judges security by absolute weight alone

options.text: Pier one, because it resists the smallest thrust and so has the least capacity to spare
options.misconception: judges security by thrust size alone

options.text: Pier two, because it needs 180 kN of weight to balance the moment but has only 240 kN, the smallest margin
All three equally, because the ratio of weight to thrust is the same measure in every case
options.misconception: ignores the height and lever arm in the comparison

questions.explanation: Required weight is thrust times height over lever arm: 125, 180 and 61.5 kN. Against actual weights of 200, 240 and 150 kN the margins are 75, 60 and 88.5 kN, so pier two is least secure.
questions.hint: Compare the required weight with the actual weight.

questions.topic: Why a tensioned concrete beam spans further
questions.learningObjective: Separate the action of prestressing from that of ordinary reinforcement
questions.stem: Two questions are put to the engineer: what the tendons do to the concrete before the load arrives, and what remains the concrete's own job afterwards.

options.text: They replace the concrete's cement binder, while the ordinary reinforcement carries the surface finish
options.misconception: treats tendons as a substitute for the binder

options.text: They stretch the concrete so it resists compression, while the ordinary reinforcement carries the dead load
options.misconception: reverses which stress the tendons induce

options.text: They stiffen the tendons themselves, while the ordinary reinforcement carries the weight of the slab
options.misconception: credits the tendons with stiffening themselves

options.text: They compress the concrete so it resists bending, while ordinary reinforcement carries the tension that remains

questions.explanation: Prestressing compresses the concrete before load arrives, so flexural tension at the soffit is offset and the section can be shallow. Ordinary reinforcement then carries the tension and shear remaining.

questions.topic: What distinguishes the three classical orders
questions.learningObjective: Identify the Corinthian order from a capital with carved leaves
questions.stem: A curator's survey card for a capital shows two rows of curled leaves rising from a smooth stem, with small shoots at the corners. Which order does the card describe?

options.misconception: confuses acanthus leaves with Ionic scrolls

options.text: Corinthian, whose capital of acanthus leaves is its clearest single identifying feature
Doric, whose plain cushion capital is the earliest and simplest form
options.misconception: confuses the carved capital with the plain one

options.text: Composite, which mixes the leaves of Corinthian with the scrolls of Ionic in one capital
options.misconception: confuses Corinthian with the Composite order

questions.topic: A colonnade on three sides
questions.learningObjective: Identify Doric and Ionic porticoes from a written survey record

stimulus.body: A survey record compares two porticoes at a coastal site. The first has columns with no base, fluted shafts meeting sharp ridges, plain cushion capitals and a frieze broken by small panels and rounded discs. The second has columns with moulded bases, plain shafts, capitals carved with scrolls and a frieze of one continuous unbroken band. The note asks the survey team to record which orders are present.

questions.stem: Which orders do the two porticoes in the survey record represent?

options.text: The first is Corinthian and the second Doric, told apart by base, capital and frieze pattern
options.misconception: names the first portico Corinthian

options.text: The first is Ionic and the second Doric, told apart by base, capital and frieze pattern
options.misconception: reverses the two orders in the record

options.text: The first is Doric and the second Ionic, told apart by base, capital and frieze pattern
The first is Doric and the second Corinthian, told apart by base, capital and frieze pattern
options.misconception: names the second portico Corinthian

questions.explanation: A base-less shaft, sharp arrises and a frieze broken into triglyphs and metopes belong to Doric. Moulded bases, scroll capitals and a continuous frieze belong to Ionic.
questions.hint: Check base, capital and frieze together.

questions.learningObjective: Compare bearing pressures under equal column loads
questions.stem: A record of settlement at the foot of a surveyed colonnade shows three columns with base plates of 0.8, 1.2 and 2.0 square metres carrying equal axial loads. Which column bears the least pressure on the pavement?

options.text: All three equally, because equal axial loads always produce equal bearing pressures
options.misconception: ignores the differing bearing areas

options.text: The first, because the smallest base keeps the load close to the column and therefore the ground
options.misconception: assumes a small base spreads the load further

options.text: The second, because a base of intermediate size suits the middle of the colonnade
options.misconception: chooses the base by position rather than area

options.text: The third, because the largest base area spreads the same load over the greatest area

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the pediment closes
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the tympanum was chosen for the principal relief
questions.stem: In a field note on a temple front, explain why the pediment's flat inner field was the chosen place for the temple's chief relief.

answer.exemplar: The tympanum is the one large, flat and untwisted surface in the whole elevation, bounded by the horizontal cornice below and the two sloping cornices above. A sculptor can carve into such a field in high relief without the forms being cut off by a moulding, and the field is seen from below at a distance, which is exactly the condition that suits a row of large figures. By contrast the frieze and the architrave are narrow bands interrupted by triglyphs and metopes, which break up any composition placed on them. The pediment therefore acts as the frame that makes the front's principal image legible.

questions.explanation: The tympanum is the one large flat surface in the elevation, bounded by the cornices, so a sculptor can carve deep figures into it unhindered. The narrow frieze below is broken up and holds no composition.
questions.hint: Think about what a flat field allows.

options.misconception: ends the thrust at the wrong member

options.misconception: ends the thrust at the pinnacle

questions.explanation: The thrust leaves the vault at the springing, crosses the aisle in the flying buttress and reaches the outer pier, whose weight carries it into the ground. The clerestory and rib lie inside the vault.

questions.learningObjective: Express the depth saved by prestressing as a percentage
questions.stem: A thrust estimate in the survey of a market hall gives a prestressed beam a span of 24 m with a depth of 1.0 m, while the plain concrete alternative for the same span is 1.6 m deep. What percentage of the plain beam's depth has been saved?
questions.explanation: The saving is 1.6 minus 1.0, which is 0.6 m, and 0.6 over 1.6 is 0.375, or thirty-seven and a half per cent. Measuring the saving against the shallower depth would give 60 per cent.
questions.hint: Divide the saving by the original depth.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The force a flying buttress takes
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a flying buttress and its outer pier work together
questions.stem: In a field report on the surveyed church, explain how the flying buttress and the outer pier work together to make a vault safe.

answer.exemplar: The vault pushes outwards at its springing, and a flying buttress is a raking half-arch that takes that thrust at the top and carries it across the aisle to an outer pier. The pier is a mass of masonry whose own weight holds it down, so the thrust cannot overturn it. The thrust then passes down the pier into the ground, and the combination of a light flyer and a heavy pier lets the wall between them be opened up with windows. Neither element works alone: the flyer alone would have nothing to push against, and the pier alone would have nothing to react.

questions.explanation: The flying buttress takes the vault's outward thrust and carries it to the outer pier, whose weight stops it overturning. The flyer alone has nothing to push against, and the pier alone nothing to react.
questions.hint: Think of a strut and a counterweight.

questions.stem: The survey computes the height of an Ionic column from a measured shaft diameter of 0.70 m and the Ionic ratio of eight shaft diameters to the total height. What is the total height in metres?
questions.explanation: An Ionic column stands about eight shaft diameters tall, so 8 x 0.70 m gives 5.60 m. The Doric ratio of six would give 4.2 m and the Corinthian ten would give 7.0 m for the same shaft.
questions.hint: Multiply the diameter by eight.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A colonnade on three sides
questions.learningObjective: Interpret an entablature that runs round and dies into the wall
questions.stem: A survey of a portico finds that the entablature resting on the columns continues round both flanks and dies into the wall at the far end of each return. Which reading does that support?

options.text: The entablature was carried round the flanks so that the temple could be entered on every side
options.misconception: turns a construction detail into a doorway claim

options.text: The portico was rebuilt as a separate structure after the rest of the building was finished
options.misconception: invents a later rebuilding of the portico

options.text: The colonnade is a continuous screen that carries the roof edge all the way round to the solid wall
The walls behind were planned as screens of masonry rather than as solid enclosures
options.misconception: draws a conclusion about the walls' solidity

questions.explanation: An entablature that runs round and dies into the wall shows the colonnade as one continuous element turning the corner, with the wall as the solid end. It implies nothing about entrances.
questions.hint: Follow the beam round the corner.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a podium and a single stair achieve
questions.learningObjective: Read a sanctuary platform and flight as levelling and approach

stimulus.body: A survey of a hillside sanctuary records that the building stands on a stone platform raised about 2 m above the terrace, and that a single flight of wide steps climbs the platform on the axis of the front. The steps are the only way onto the platform, and a shallow channel runs along the foot of them to the valley. The note records that the builders of the sanctuary left the platform's outer edge plain and undecorated, while the top of the flight and the doorway above it were heavily carved.

questions.stem: Which pair of functions does the survey record describe for the platform and the stair?

options.text: The platform displays the carved sculptures, and the stair takes visitors around the outside of the building
options.misconception: mislocates the carving on the platform

options.text: The platform stores water for the builders, and the stair divides the visitors into two queues
options.misconception: reads the platform as a water store

options.text: The platform provides extra rooms beneath the building, and the stair leads to the upper storey
options.misconception: invents rooms below the platform

options.text: The platform lifts and isolates the building above the ground, and the stair concentrates entry on one axis

questions.explanation: Raising the sanctuary on a platform levels it above the uneven rock, and a single wide flight on the doorway's axis concentrates entry on one door. The carving at the top of the flight confirms the intended route.
questions.hint: Read the carving and the level change.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the pediment closes
questions.learningObjective: Compare the fields of two measured pediment fronts
questions.stem: A comparison of two fronts from the survey records the first with a pediment base of 7 m and a height of 2.1 m, and the second with a base of 9 m and a height of 1.8 m. Which front has the larger triangular field?

options.text: The first, whose field of 7.35 square metres is larger than the 8.10 of the second
options.misconception: judges by the taller pediment alone

options.text: The second, whose field of 8.10 square metres is larger than the 7.35 of the first
They are equal, because the two pediments are seen from the same distance by the survey team
options.misconception: lets viewing distance decide the area

options.text: The first, because the height of the pediment matters more than its width in every case
options.misconception: insists height always dominates area

questions.explanation: Half the base times the height gives 7.35 square metres for the first front and 8.10 for the second. The wider pediment wins although it is the shallower, because area depends on the product.
questions.hint: Compute half base times height for each.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The force a flying buttress takes
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a flying buttress is curved rather than a straight prop
questions.stem: In a note to the survey team, explain why the flying buttress is shaped as a raking arch rather than a straight prop.

answer.exemplar: A straight prop leaning against the wall would press on it at an angle and could push the wall outwards, transferring the very thrust the buttress is meant to remove. A raking arch is curved so that the line of the thrust runs down its length in compression, exactly as it does in a standing arch, and the force arrives at the outer pier down a path that pushes into it rather than sideways. That is why the buttress looks like a flying arch and behaves like an arch with only one half of its ring present.

questions.explanation: A straight prop pushes on the wall instead of carrying the thrust away. A raking arch keeps the thrust in compression down its curve into the outer pier, delivering the force into the pier, not the wall.
questions.hint: Think about where the thrust line runs.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a tensioned concrete beam spans further
questions.learningObjective: Explain prestressing and the anchorage that holds it
questions.stem: Two questions are put to the engineer: why a prestressed beam can be shallower than a plain one, and what has to happen to the tendon before the load arrives.

options.text: The tendons shorten the span, and they must be inspected after the pour to confirm the length
options.misconception: treats the tendon as a span shortener

options.text: The tendons lighten the beam, and they must be warmed before the load arrives to avoid shock
options.misconception: invents a warming step in the sequence

options.text: The tendons compress the concrete so it resists bending, and they must be tensioned and anchored to hold that force
The tendons stiffen the aggregate, and they must be grouted before the beam is lifted into place
options.misconception: credits the tendon with stiffening aggregate

questions.explanation: Prestressing puts the concrete into compression before load arrives, so the flexural tension that sets a plain beam's depth never arises. The force exists only while the tendon is stretched and anchored.
questions.hint: Ask what compression does and what holds it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a column has base, shaft and capital
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the effective length of a cantilever column
questions.stem: A camp calculation treats a free-standing stone column 5 m tall as a cantilever for the purpose of buckling. What effective length in metres does that assumption give?
questions.explanation: A cantilever is fixed at one end and free at the other, so its effective length is twice the real length: 2 x 5 m gives 10 m. A column fixed at both ends would be taken as 5 m instead.
questions.hint: Double the real length for a cantilever.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What distinguishes the three classical orders
questions.learningObjective: Weigh a capital against a frieze when they point to different orders
questions.stem: The survey team notes a capital carved with leaves, a slender shaft, and a frieze with no triglyphs or metopes at all. Which conclusion is sound?

options.text: The capital points to Corinthian, and the plain frieze means the building has no order at all
options.misconception: denies the building any coherent order

options.text: The capital points to Doric, so the plain frieze simply confirms that the order is Doric throughout
options.misconception: reads leaves as a Doric capital

options.text: The capital points to Ionic, and the plain frieze shows the sculptor ran out of time
options.misconception: reads scrolls into a leaf carving

options.text: The capital points to Corinthian, but a plain frieze shows the building does not follow one order strictly

questions.explanation: Carved leaves identify the Corinthian capital, while the frieze belongs to the order governing the elevation. Where the two disagree, the building was assembled from different workshops.
questions.hint: Read the capital and the frieze separately.
